sources.title: Invented household waste-count worksheet
sources.limitations: Counts are fabricated, have no observed households, and exclude displaced burdens.

sources.title: Imaginary object-reuse options table
sources.limitations: Costs and alternatives are invented and do not establish material lifecycle effects.

sources.title: Fictional access-design checklist
sources.limitations: The exercise has no interviews with disabled people or actual accessibility audit.

sources.title: Invented public-service navigation rehearsal
sources.limitations: No municipality, program, applicant or service is represented.

sources.title: Fictional habitat learning scenario
sources.limitations: No ecological site, wildlife data or environmental measurement exists.

sources.title: Imaginary accountability compact evaluation
sources.limitations: No real company, affected people or independent reviewer participated.

sources.title: Invented workshop participation table
sources.limitations: Figures are illustrative; no meeting, facilitator or participant exists.

claims.title: A fictional pantry checklist is completed
claims.statement: In an invented scenario, a participant ticks a storage checklist and marks a learning exercise complete.
claims.method: A made-up scenario marks an activity; there is no observation, identity or performance evaluation.
claims.limitations: Completing a checklist cannot establish reduced waste, safe storage or a household outcome.
claims.alternative_explanations: The checkbox could be wrong, incomplete or unrelated to changes in actual food handling.

claims.title: A hypothetical checklist produces a plan
claims.statement: An imaginary learner writes three proposed waste-prevention ideas as an output, without acting on them.
claims.method: The fixture counts a written output in the imagined food literacy exercise only.
claims.limitations: Three notes do not imply that any people took action, and the metric is invented.
claims.alternative_explanations: Notes might repeat existing ideas or create impractical, unsafe or high-cost plans.

claims.title: Invented before-after food-waste totals
claims.statement: A hypothetical seven-day waste count changes from 40 to 30 invented items after an imagined planning intervention.
claims.method: No uncontrolled real-world study occurred; fabricated totals demonstrate how an unjustified outcome claim can arise.
claims.limitations: A fictional reduction of ten units cannot demonstrate causal benefit or food safety.
claims.alternative_explanations: Changing attendance, menu, purchasing, counting methods, seasonality or disposal pathways could explain observed differences if these were real.

claims.title: Compare reuse routes without asserting benefit
claims.statement: A fictional reuse decision grid proposes comparing repair, sharing and disposal on cost, effort and lifecycle uncertainty.
claims.method: A worksheet lists options and questions; no repair or measured effect occurs.
claims.limitations: An option list does not establish that reuse has a smaller footprint than alternatives.
claims.alternative_explanations: Repair travel, materials, storage, energy or user safety could overturn a tentative preference.

claims.title: Proposed access alternatives in a mock workshop
claims.statement: An invented facilitator describes three alternative ways to participate without actually recruiting anybody.
claims.method: This synthetic fixture tallies alternatives written in an imaginary workshop plan; there is no actual usability or participation measurement.
claims.limitations: Counting alternatives says nothing about usability or whether people feel welcome or protected.
claims.alternative_explanations: Participation modes may be inaccessible in practice or add hidden labor and privacy costs.

claims.title: A plain-language navigator may reduce confusion
claims.statement: A fictional public-service navigation guide might help a reader, but the effect is purely hypothetical.
claims.method: A conceptual hypothesis is recorded without interviews, causal comparisons or service-use data.
claims.limitations: The guide has no official standing; inaccurate requirements could mislead people.
claims.alternative_explanations: Access barriers may stem from eligibility, bureaucracy, inaccessible websites or other factors.

claims.title: A habitat concept may introduce ecological harm
claims.statement: A hypothetical planting idea might unintentionally harm a habitat if species or site permissions are wrong.
claims.method: The imaginary exercise explicitly examines possible adverse outcomes and stop conditions.
claims.limitations: No species identification, site evaluation, ecological permit or real harm assessment exists.
claims.alternative_explanations: Changing climate, local species interactions and land management may require entirely different interventions.

claims.title: Independent review is part of an imaginary compact
claims.statement: An imagined institution outlines measurable changes and external scrutiny, but no agreement or remediation exists.
claims.method: Fictional clauses are drafted to test accountability and correction pathways.
claims.limitations: A draft compact is not consent, implementation, independent verification or institutional rehabilitation.
claims.alternative_explanations: Other reforms, enforceable remedies or replacement services may be more appropriate.

claims.title: Invented attendance versus inclusion comparison
claims.statement: A made-up workshop increases attendance from eight to twelve fictional visits, which does not prove improved inclusion.
claims.method: The fictional before-after visits intentionally demonstrate a weak proxy for accessibility.
claims.limitations: Attendance totals reveal nothing about participant autonomy, retention, unmet needs, exclusion or coercion.
claims.alternative_explanations: Publicity, convenience, repeated visits, forced attendance or changes in counting could alter totals.

claims.title: Withdrawn claim: sample engagement equals trust
claims.statement: An earlier fictional draft incorrectly equated illustrative clicks with residents trusting public institutions.
claims.method: The specimen remains visible to demonstrate withdrawal records without preserving an approved interpretation.
claims.limitations: Clicks are neither consent nor independently measured public trust; this example is withdrawn.
claims.alternative_explanations: Automated clicks, interface design or nonrepresentative interest may produce activity without confidence.

events.reason: Clarify that hypothetical attendance counts cannot establish inclusive participation or causal benefit.
Withdraw an invalid fictional proxy that confused website clicks with public trust or consent.
